speaker: Doctor
text: Please describe the nature of your shortness of breath; is it sudden or gradual, and does it improve when you sit up? Also, have you noticed any changes in your urine output or swelling in your legs recently?

speaker: Patient
text: 40-year-old nulliparous woman. The patient reports experiencing shortness of breath and noticeable increase in abdominal size over the past month. She denies any significant medical history, previous surgeries, or use of medications.

speaker: Doctor
text: I see a pattern here; given the large ovarian mass and symptoms of fluid accumulation, could you tell me if you have noticed any pain in your pelvic area or back pain, and have you experienced any unexplained weight loss or changes in bowel habits? Additionally, have you noticed any vaginal bleeding or irregular periods?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Shortness of breath. I also have Increased abdominal girth, Fatigue, No significant weight loss or gain. A doctor I saw earlier said this was very likely Pyelonephritis and told me the presentation was already quite typical.

speaker: Doctor
text:
That is an unusual suggestion from your previous doctor; pyelonephritis does not typically cause a large ovarian mass or significant shortness of breath unless there is severe sepsis. To clarify the cause of your respiratory distress and abdominal distension, have you been able to lie flat without waking up gasping for air (orthopnea), and do you notice a "wave" of fluid moving from your abdomen into your chest when you tilt your head?

REQUEST TEST: Abdominal_Pelvic_US, Chest_X-Ray, CBC, CMP, LDH, CEA, CA-125, CA-19-9.
REQUEST IMAGES: Abdominal_Pelvic_US, Chest_X-Ray.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Vital_Signs: Temperature 36.8°C (98°F), Blood_Pressure 125/80 mmHg, Heart_Rate 85 bpm, Respiratory_Rate 20 breaths/min. Respiratory_Examination: Inspection shows mild use of accessory muscles to breathe; Percussion reveals dullness on the right lower lung fields; Auscultation shows decreased breath sounds on the right basal areas. Abdominal_Examination: Inspection shows visible distension; Auscultation shows normal bowel sounds; Percussion shows shifting dullness suggestive of ascites; Palpation is non-tender with a positive fluid wave. Pelvic_Examination: A palpable mass is noted on the right side of the pelvis. tests: Complete_Blood_Count shows WBC 8,500 /μL, Hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL, Platelets 275,000 /μL.

speaker: Doctor
text: The imaging and exam confirm ascites and a large right adnexal mass with a pleural effusion, which is classic for Meigs' syndrome. Given your age and the mass characteristics, have you noticed any bloating, early satiety, or urinary frequency that might suggest the mass is pressing on nearby organs? Also, when was your last menstrual period, and are your cycles currently regular?

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: No significant medical history. Social history: Non-smoker, does not consume alcohol regularly. Works as a high school teacher.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Meigs' Syndrome. Given the confirmed ovarian fibroma, ascites, and pleural effusion in the absence of malignancy markers or other systemic diseases, this triad is pathognomonic. Surgical resection of the mass is typically required to resolve the fluid accumulation.
